7819adf1a0.title: Opinion | What Happens When the Economy Becomes Dependent on AI?
7819adf1a0.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly widespread and embedded in decisions involving credit, investment, production, financial markets and infrastructure, managing the risks associated with its use is becoming more important than ever. The debate surrounding artificial intelligence is no longer confined to its ability to write texts, analyse data or help people perform tasks more quickly. The world has entered a new phase in which AI is gradually moving to the heart of economic decision-making. Banks use it to assess credit applications and detect fraud, companies rely on it for pricing and production, financial markets deploy algorithms for trading, and institutions use it to analyse risks and inform their decisions. The most important economic question, therefore, is no longer simply what artificial intelligence can do, but what happens when the economy itself becomes increasingly dependent on it. This question has become more pressing as AI capabilities advance rapidly and governments and major companies around the world turn greater attention to safety, oversight and governance. This does not mean that artificial intelligence has become a threat to be feared. Quite the opposite: it could become one of the most important drivers of productivity growth over the coming decades by reducing costs, improving business efficiency, enhancing data analysis, accelerating decision-making and facilitating the development of new products and services. However, economic history teaches us that every major productive force also creates new forms of risk. And that is where the real challenge begins. If a single company uses an AI system and that system fails, the company may face an operational problem. But what happens when thousands of companies, banks and institutions depend on the same limited number of models, technology providers or data centres? At that point, the problem shifts from an internal institutional issue to a potential disruption affecting a substantial part of the economy. Artificial intelligence may make the economy more efficient, but it could also make it increasingly dependent on a limited number of companies providing AI models, cloud computing services, semiconductors and data centres. The greater this dependence becomes, the greater the possibility that a problem affecting one of these critical components could spread simultaneously across numerous institutions. 35ec487175.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring. "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. 8e9eaa53a3.summary: California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the company of putting the public at risk by failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence. The lawsuit is the latest broadside at the company, which — along with other tech industry players — has faced scrutiny over a rush to develop A.I. at the potential expense of consumer safety. In a 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, the state said OpenAI’s lax safeguards led to cyberattacks by its A.I. products during testing, including a breach this year when OpenAI’s agents went rogue and attacked the A.I. start-up Hugging Face’s systems . The move is the latest effort by a state to rein in the power of A.I. companies in the face of growing concerns about the technology’s ability to go rogue. b7ebb93ddb.title: Google DeepMind researchers verify Signal’s cryptographic core with AlphaProof Code
b7ebb93ddb.summary: Google DeepMind researchers have used AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal messaging protocol, connecting cryptographic guarantees to compiled machine code. The work uses AlphaProof Code, a framework that combines human-directed specification writing with teams of agents that generate proofs checked by Lean, a programming language and proof assistant. The researchers describe the result as the first verification of protocol-level security properties for a widely deployed, unmodified cryptographic protocol implementation at this depth. Their paper, published on November 10, examines the code within a defined execution environment and sets out the assumptions and limitations behind its guarantees. Five researchers directed the proof work over four weeks in October 2026. The paper says none of the authors wrote the proof code themselves. The team worked with libsignal’s production Rust code, compiling it within a command-line program for AArch64 Linux, an Arm-based computing environment. The verification covers the protocol’s PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet components. The security properties examined include authentication, forward secrecy and post-compromise security, addressing how messages remain protected under specified scenarios involving exposed keys or compromised devices. Much previous protocol analysis has examined mathematical designs, specially written implementations or narrower properties of production software. AlphaProof Code’s research connects security statements to the compiled implementation, where differences between a design and the code that executes it can introduce vulnerabilities. The researchers used two established approaches. A symbolic model treats cryptographic operations abstractly, while a computational model bounds an attacker’s chances of success under assumptions about the underlying cryptography. To test whether the specifications could identify insecure behavior, the team reintroduced two previously fixed libsignal bugs into separate experimental builds. In both cases, the agents produced Lean-checked proofs that the altered implementation violated the symbolic security theorem. These were tests using historical bugs, rather than announcements of newly discovered vulnerabilities in the current software. f5b8e45b4a.summary: China's Baidu reported on Monday quarterly revenue in line with market estimates as weakness in its core advertising division offset strong demand for its AI cloud computing services. US-listed shares of Baidu were down more than 1% in premarket trading. Baidu has been spending heavily to expand in cloud computing as enterprisesboost spending on artificial intelligence. That spending helped lift revenue at Baidu's AI-linked business segment by 37% to 13.2 billion yuan ($1.98 billion). AI cloud infrastructure revenue alone surged 94% to 8.2 billion yuan in the quarter ended September 30. But investors worry that Baidu is falling behind AI rivals such as e-commerce leader Alibaba and startups like DeepSeek and Moonshot due to the lack of major upgrades to its Ernie AI model. Baidu previewed its Ernie 5.5 Flash model this month, touting its capabilities in coding, 3D modelling and content creation. However, the preview attracteda far more muted public response than previous Ernie iterations. Still, performance in AI-related services has helped make up for slowing demand in Baidu's staple online advertising business, where advertisers have tightened budgets as weak consumer spending weighs on the economy. Baidu's online marketing services revenue slid 22% to 11.9 billion yuan in the quarter. The internet search major reported July-September revenue of 30.81 billion yuan ($4.62 billion), versus the 30.86 billion yuan average of 15 analyst estimates compiled by LSEG. Baidu reported an adjusted profit of 6.78 yuan per American Depositary Share, beating estimates of 6.36 yuan, helped by a decline in overall costs. Adding Arabic would also help make the system accessible to other Arab countries in the future, he said. Khattab noted that the cooperation reflects the strong scientific and technical partnership between the Jordanian and Chinese meteorological authorities. He said it strengthens the Kingdom's readiness for extreme weather and supports national efforts to reduce disaster risk and protect lives and property. Ahmed Rahhou, minister of artificial intelligence, digital transformation and administrative reform, presented the ministry’s first budget to the interior committee of the House of Representatives on 10 November, Express TV reported . Rahhou, formerly head of the Competition Council, joined the government formed in October; a decree on 26 October gave him responsibility for national AI policy, Médias24 reported . The committee’s written report, seen by the Arabic-language news site Hespress and reported on Monday, says Morocco expects to issue “the first open-source national language model”, with early trials to adapt a model to Darija, a Moroccan benchmark for evaluating models and a model to read Moroccan Arabic manuscripts. Quotes are translated from Arabic. The work draws on national datasets that include about 300mn text tokens, 150 gigabytes of documents, 10,000 hours of transcribed Darija audio, the official gazette archive from 1913 to 2026 and about 90,000 legal texts, according to the report. The ministry’s predecessor worked with the French company Mistral AI on open-source tools for Darija under the “Maroc IA 2030” roadmap, the government portal Maroc.ma said . The committee report says that partnership produced an open speech-recognition model. For Morocco AI in public services, the ministry’s “Idarati” assistant, built on about 2,800 administrative procedures and analysis of some 10,000 legal texts, is to gain a voice version and an agent that follows a citizen’s request through to the result. Amazigh support will be added to a meeting assistant that already transcribes Darija. A legal assistant and a guide for entrepreneurs are also planned. 862f2dd495.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
862f2dd495.summary: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. Key features: Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.” Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.” Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”. Results : The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point…
